segments.title: The scenario and the five rules
sections: Right About The Market, Wrong About The Morning
Where Each Hard Rule Came From

cues.text: You marked the level. You wrote the idea. Price did what you said it would. And the session still ended worse than the read deserved.
Somewhere between 9:30 a.m. and 11 a.m., the trades stopped coming from the plan and started coming from you.
A second entry, taken because the first was easy. A stop-out, your stop hit, answered forty seconds later. An exit, because a red candle looked big.
Your read was right. The chart agreed with it. The order ticket had other plans.
That gap, between a right read, your written call on what price does at the level, and the trades you place, is what this module is about.
Discipline will not close it. Discipline is what working mechanisms look like from the outside.
So every mistake here gets three things.
One: what it looks like.
Two: what it reveals about you.
Three: a mechanism that fixes it. A setting, a written line, a rehearsed routine, or a journal field.
Now, where each hard rule came from. The five rules in Module 2 look like restrictions. Each is the written answer to something traders do to themselves on a bad day.
One: the trading window, the hours an entry is allowed. It stops the late entry taken because the level was right there.
Two: the news windows, the minutes around a release. They stop a trade turning into a bet on a number.
Three: the four reasons to flatten by hand. They stop exits on hope, on sunk cost, on a mood.
Four: the 2R kill switch, the daily loss limit at your broker, twice the risk on one trade. It stops you negotiating with your own limit.
Five: the post-loss reset, the routine after a loss. It stops the next trade coming from the last one.
The rule: keep the rules as written, and when one feels like a cost, read the behaviour it stops, not the rule.
Getting it wrong is bargaining. The window is for normal days. The reset is for big losses. It reveals you read a rule as a price, not a decision already made.
The fix: write what each rule stops, in your own words, on a card beside your screen, and read it aloud before the first order.
The rule does not get tired at 2:30 p.m. Attention does. That is the whole argument.

segments.title: Breaks and the reset
sections: The Post-Loss Reset Is A Rehearsed Skill

cues.text: A scheduled break is written on your plan before the session, at a fixed time, and taken whether the session is going well or badly.
Never triggered by a result. A pause after a loss is a different thing, coming up next.
Attention drains with screen time. A break at a fixed time is the cheapest repair there is: platform closed, away from the desk, back to the plan.
A break carries no promise. It is hygiene, like sleep. It is not a cure.
After a day or more away, the first session starts with the full pre-market routine, the sheet you build before the open, and one rehearsal of the reset before the first order.
The rule: breaks sit on the plan at fixed times and are taken whatever the result.
Getting it wrong is skipping the 11 a.m. break because the morning is green. It reveals your P and L runs your breaks.
The fix: an alarm for each, and the platform closed when it rings. Your screen will survive fifteen minutes without you. It has survived worse.
Now, the post-loss reset: the routine after every losing trade, before any new entry. It is a skill, built by repetition in the conditions it is for.
A routine you have only run while calm, you have never run at all. After a stop-out your pulse is up and your hand is already on the order ticket.
One: cancel every working entry order, every entry order still resting. A working order is the impulse, already placed.
Two: the physical step. Feet flat, one long exhale, three or four rounds of box breathing.
Three: three questions, aloud. What is the chart telling me? Are any setups forming? What would need to happen for one to appear?
Four: write the third answer in one line in your journal, your record of every trade. A blank line means no trade.
Once a week, with no position on, rehearse it with your heart rate up, straight after a flight of stairs. Count the rehearsals in the journal.
The rule: after every loss, the full reset before any new entry, rehearsed weekly.
Getting it wrong is a reset run at the screen with the chart still moving, or skipped because it was only a small loss.
It reveals the reset is a mood to wait out, not a routine to run. With no rehearsals behind it, it is a plan, not a skill.

segments.title: The first win, and the losing run
sections: The Re-entry Loop After A First Win
Losing Is A Member Of A Distribution

cues.text: The re-entry loop is a run of entries, one after another, without a fresh setup, a level and a read together. It starts after the first win, not a loss.
The first trade wins. Easy feels like information. The next entry comes a little faster, a little further from a level.
Nothing about the market said the second trade was better. The first result did. A win is not a forecast. It is a receipt.
Now, the four checks. The second trade faces the same test as the first, written before the order.
One: the location is a named level, a price marked before the session.
Two: the trigger, the price event that puts you in, fired before entry.
Three: the stop is behind structure, past the level, not a fixed count of points.
Four: the size matches the plan for that stop. Two checks or fewer is a grade C, the lowest grade, and a C is not taken.
The rule: every entry after the first, especially the first after a win, gets the four checks written before the order goes in.
Getting it wrong is a second entry from mid-range, the space between levels, minutes after the first trade closed, grade filled in afterwards.
It reveals the first win was read as a forecast. That grade describes what you did. It was never a test.
Now, losing. If a read is right most of the time, the misses are not mistakes. They are the rest of the distribution.
A plan trade that hits its stop did what the plan said it might.
Losses arrive in runs. Even with every trade independent, over a few dozen trades, three in a row is the ordinary case.
Two errors sit either side of a losing run. One: reading it as a verdict, changing the plan after three trades.
Two: reading it as nothing, when each loss carried a Broke Rule tag, the tag for a hard rule broken. That is not a distribution. It is a habit.
The rule: a plan trade that lost gets no negative tag, and setups are judged in cohorts, groups of trades sharing a setup, on the review schedule, never after a run.
Getting it wrong is tagging a plan loss as a bad entry. It reveals you are grading outcomes. Tag at the exit from the checks and the flatten reasons, never from the R column.

segments.title: Curious or needing, and the only failure

cues.text: There are two ways to sit down in front of a chart.
Curious: you want to see what the market does at your levels, and you would be content to watch it do something you cannot trade.
Needing: you want something from the session. A green day, a loss repaid, being right about an earlier idea, or just something to happen.
The market is the same either way. What you see in it is not. Boredom is not a setup. It only dresses like one.
The readiness score puts a number on it, from 0 to 2, at the top of your pre-market sheet.
2: curious about what the market does at your levels.
1: neutral.
0: needing something from the market.
It is data for your journal, not a gate. A completed sheet clears you to trade, whatever the score.
The rule: score yourself honestly every morning, and use the score as data in the review, never as a permission or a ban in the session.
Getting it wrong is scoring a 2 every day because a 0 feels like failing, or acting on it. It reveals the score has become a verdict on you.
A measurement that is managed stops measuring. The score never touches size.
Now, the only failure. On this course, a trade lost is not a failure. A rule broken is, whether the trade made money or not.
The winning rule-break is the dangerous one. A trade from mid-range that happens to work pays you for the thing you are trying to stop. That pay is the strongest training signal there is.
That is why a winning C is a warning, not a result, and why a Broke Rule tag stays on a winner.
It also means the failure is in your control. You cannot decide whether the next trade wins. You can decide whether it was taken by the plan.
The rule: a rule broken is tagged whatever the result, and the count of broken rules is the first number of every weekly review, the fixed review of the week's journal.
Getting it wrong is leaving the tag off a winner. It reveals the result is still grading the behaviour, so the behaviour is being rewarded.
The fix is a ledger: every tagged trade, winners first, with its R and the rule it broke, totalled in R and never netted against plan trades.

check.q: Why is a winning rule-break the dangerous one?
options: It pays you for the behaviour you are trying to stop

segments.title: The mechanical fixes and the worked case
sections: The Mechanical Fixes, In One List
Worked Case: The Morning After The First Win

cues.text: Now, the mechanical fixes in one list. Each is a setting, a line, a rehearsal or a journal field.
None is a resolution to try harder. Trying harder is a wish with a gym membership.
Bargaining, trading past 2R: the card by your screen, the limit locked at the account.
Exiting on a mood: one of the four reasons, or a Too Early tag, the tag for a hand exit off the plan.
Skipped breaks, cold returns: an alarm for each break, and a return-day line on the plan.
Re-entry, a reset that never runs: the written third answer, and a weekly rehearsal.
The second trade after a win: the grade line, written first.
Forgiving a winning rule-break: the ledger, never netted.
What is not on the list is deliberate. No cap on trades, no stop after a loss count, no smaller size after a red day.
The 2R kill switch is the cap, and base R, your risk on one trade, stays fixed.
The rule: losing trades are the cost of a plan. Broken rules are the only failure.
Now, the example. A hypothetical illustration, not a trade record: a composite MNQ morning, invented prices.
At 9:22 a.m. the sheet carries two branches, written if-then plans, one long, one short, a nothing case, and a readiness score with one line why.
At 9:58 a.m., a second long looks easy from mid-range. The grade line comes first. Location, mid-range. Trigger, none. Stop, nothing behind it. A C, written, not taken.
At 10:22 a.m. the other branch fires. The grade line is written first, so whatever the trade does, it carries no negative tag.
At 10:32 a.m., after a loss, the reset: orders cancelled, feet flat, one long exhale, three questions aloud, the third answer written.
Then the 11 a.m. alarm. The break is on the plan, so it is taken, green morning or red.
Getting it wrong is the other version of the morning. Without the line at 9:58, the mid-range long goes in, and after its first loss the next entry is taken to get it back.
The kill switch would end that day at 2R down. It would not save the morning. The line at 9:58 and the reset at 10:32 did.
Two moments decided the morning: a line written before an order never placed, and a routine after a loss that sent the next trade back to the chart.

segments.title: Which is yours, the assignment, and next

cues.text: Which of these is yours? Answer from your journal, not from memory, for your last ten sessions or as many as you have. One point for each line that is true.
One: every entry after a loss has a written third answer, timestamped before it.
Two: you rehearsed the reset with your heart rate up in each of the last two weeks.
Three: no trade at grade C, and every grade line written before its order.
Four: no losing A-plus or A trade carries a negative tag.
Five: every plan had its breaks written, and every break was taken.
Six: a readiness score for every session, and no size changed because of it.
Six of six: the mechanisms are in place, and the weekly review keeps them there.
Four or five: the first false line is next week's one fix, and only that one. Under four: fix line one before your next session, and add the others one a week.
One line overrides the score. If line one is false, it is the fix, whatever the total, because every other line depends on the next trade coming from the chart.
Getting it wrong is scoring from memory. Memory agrees with how the day ended. It reveals you want a verdict, not a count. The fix: six lines from the journal, on the review day.
Your assignment. Run the post-loss reset once, with no position on, straight after a flight of stairs or a fast two-minute walk.
Cancel orders on an empty ticket. Feet flat, one long exhale, four rounds of box breathing. The three questions aloud.
Then write the third answer in your journal, with the time. That is the whole assignment.
In one line: losing trades are the cost of a plan, broken rules are the only failure, and every fix is a mechanism set before the session.
Where it goes next. Every mechanism here lands in the journal.
Module 18, Journaling and Review, teaches the tags and the weekly review where the ledger lives.
Module 16 puts the readiness score on the sheet, and Module 17 covers the hours between the open and the close.
The rules themselves are in Module 2. Module 19 holds the daily habits, and Module 21 teaches how to read a distribution from your own record.
You marked the level. Now the morning follows the plan. The chart can keep its opinions.

check.q: Where do you answer the six lines from?
options: Your journal, for your last ten sessions
check.why: Answer from the journal, because memory agrees with how the day ended.

check.q: Your score is 5. What do you do?
options: Fix every false line at once
Fix the first false line next week, and only that one
check.why: Four or five means one fix at a time, starting with the first false line.

check.q: Line one is false and the total is 5 of 6. What happens?
options: Line one is still the fix
check.why: Line one overrides the score because every other line depends on the next trade coming from the chart.

check.q: What does the assignment have you rehearse?
options: The post-loss reset, with your heart rate up and no position on
check.why: You practise the routine in a body that resembles the one you will be in when it matters.

questions.q: Which best describes discipline in this module?
options: A supply you spend through the session
What a working set of mechanisms looks like from the outside
A trait that fades with age
questions.why: Every mistake gets a mechanism: a setting, a written line, a rehearsal or a journal field.

questions.q: What is the first step of the post-loss reset?
questions.why: A working order is the impulse already placed, so entry orders go first.

questions.q: A break is skipped because the morning is green. What does that reveal?
options: Your P and L is running your breaks
questions.why: Breaks are set at fixed times and taken whatever the result.

questions.q: Why does the re-entry loop begin after a win?
options: The market turns after a win
The first win is read as information about the next trade
questions.why: Nothing about the market said the second trade was better. The first result did.

questions.q: A plan trade hits its stop. Which tag does it get?
questions.why: A trade built and exited to plan that lost carries no negative tag.

questions.q: What does the readiness score do?
questions.why: It is data, never a permission or a ban, and it never touches size.

questions.q: Which is the only failure counted on this course?
options: A rule broken, whatever the result
questions.why: A winning rule-break is the dangerous one, so the tag stays on a winner.

questions.q: What is the first number of every weekly review?
questions.why: The ledger counts broken rules first, then totals their R, and never nets them against plan trades.
